name: Prince Bandar bin Sultan

summary.text: Prince Bandar bin Sultan Al Saud was Saudi Arabia's ambassador to the United States from 1983 until King Fahd accepted his resignation in 2005. As ambassador he had signature authority over Saudi government accounts at Riggs Bank in Washington that U.S. regulators and the FBI examined in 2003-2004. The declassified 28 pages of the 2002 Joint Inquiry describe checks from his and his wife's Riggs accounts to a Saudi national, Osama Bassnan, and Bassnan's wife; the 9/11 Commission found no evidence those funds reached the plot. In 2007 British media reported that BAE Systems had paid more than £1 billion into Riggs accounts linked to him under the Al-Yamamah arms contracts; Bandar said the accounts belonged to the Saudi Ministry of Defense and Aviation and denied wrongdoing. The UK Serious Fraud Office dropped its inquiry in December 2006; BAE pleaded guilty in the U.S. in March 2010 to conspiracy and export-control charges, not bribery.

facts.claim: Bandar served as Saudi ambassador to the United States for more than 20 years, from 1983 to 2005. In July 2005 the Saudi Foreign Ministry said he had asked King Fahd to relieve him of his duties for private reasons 'after more than 20 years of distinguished service'; Al Jazeera reported that the king accepted the resignation and that Prince Turki al-Faisal would replace him.
facts.quote: Bandar had asked the king to relieve him of his duties for private reasons "after more than 20 years of distinguished service"

facts.claim: The Washington Post reported on April 7, 2004 that the FBI was investigating banking transactions by Saudi officials at Riggs Bank, including millions of dollars in deposits and withdrawals made in December 2003 by Bandar; Riggs compliance staff asked a representative of the ambassador to explain them, and when he declined, Riggs reported the activity as suspicious to the Treasury Department and ended its relationship with the Saudi embassy.
facts.quote: including millions of dollars in deposits and withdrawals made in December by the Saudi ambassador, Prince Bandar bin Sultan

sources.title: Saudi Money at Riggs Probed

facts.claim: Newsweek reported that a federal probe of the Saudi embassy's Riggs accounts uncovered large overseas wire transfers by Bandar, including $17.4 million over four months from the Saudi Defense Ministry account to an individual in Saudi Arabia described as coordinating home improvements and construction for Bandar, which a Riggs suspicious activity report of November 2003 tied to a new palace, and a $400,000 wire from a Riggs account to an overseas luxury-car dealer. A Riggs compliance officer said it was impossible to distinguish government funds from personal purposes.
facts.quote: In another instance, Bandar wired $400,000 from a Riggs account to a luxury-car dealer overseas.

sources.title: Bandar and the $2 Billion Question
Exclusive: New Questions About Saudi Money, and Bandar

facts.claim: The declassified 28 pages of the 2002 Joint Inquiry state that, according to the FBI, on May 14, 1998 Osama Bassnan cashed a $15,000 check from Bandar, and that Bassnan's wife cashed a $10,000 check from Bandar's wife on January 8, 1998. They also describe 31 cashier's checks totaling $74,000 (February 1999 to May 2002) payable to Bassnan's wife from the Riggs account of Bandar's wife, some of which the FBI determined went to the wife of Omar al-Bayoumi. The Joint Inquiry said further investigation could reveal legitimate and innocent explanations.
facts.quote: According to the FBI, on May 14, 1998, Bassnan cashed a check from Bandar in the amount of $15,000.

facts.claim: The 9/11 Commission stated that it found no evidence that Saudi Princess Haifa al Faisal provided any funds to the conspiracy, either directly or indirectly, and that, contrary to highly publicized allegations, it found no evidence that the hijackers Hazmi or Mihdhar received money from Osama Bassnan. The FBI and CIA concluded that no member of the Saudi royal family knowingly supported the attacks.
facts.quote: We have found no evidence that Saudi Princess Haifa al Faisal provided any funds to the conspiracy, either directly or indirectly.

sources.title: '28 pages': Indirect 9/11 link to Saudi Arabia's Bandar revealed
Selected Revelations from the Declassified 28 Pages on 9/11

facts.claim: In November 2002, after reports of the Haifa checks, Saudi foreign policy adviser Adel al-Jubeir said on television that it was 'preposterous' and 'outrageous' to suggest that Princess Haifa had any role in funding terrorism, and embassy sources described the payments as typical royal-family charity; Princess Haifa told the New York Times: 'All I wanted to do was to give some help to someone in need.'
facts.quote: a high-ranking Saudi official, Adel al-Jubeir, said in television interviews yesterday that it was "preposterous" and "outrageous" to suggest that Princess Haifa had any role in funding terrorism

facts.claim: In June 2007 the BBC and the Guardian reported that BAE Systems had made payments, put at up to $2 billion (more than £1 billion) over a decade, into a Washington bank account controlled by Bandar in connection with the Al-Yamamah military aircraft contracts between Britain and Saudi Arabia. Newsweek reported that the payments went through the Saudi Defense Ministry's Riggs accounts over which Bandar had signature authority.
facts.quote: The BBC and Guardian newspaper reported last week that BAE Systems made "secret" payments to a Washington, D.C., bank account controlled by Bandar.

sources.title: Bandar and the $2 Billion Question
The Case of the Well-Placed Prince
UK arms firm denies secret payments

facts.claim: Bandar, through a London law firm in June 2007, denied wrongdoing over the BAE payments, stating: 'The accounts at Riggs Bank were in the name of the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Defense and Aviation (MODA)', that any BAE payments into them were pursuant to the Al-Yamamah contracts and not secret from the parties, that the accounts were audited annually by Saudi Finance Ministry staff, and that although he was an authorised signatory, money leaving the accounts was used only for ministry-approved purposes. BAE said the Al-Yamamah arrangement was government-to-government and denied wrongdoing.
facts.quote: The accounts at Riggs Bank were in the name of the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Defense and Aviation (MODA)

sources.title: The Case of the Well-Placed Prince

facts.claim: On December 14, 2006, UK Attorney General Lord Goldsmith told the House of Lords that the Director of the Serious Fraud Office had decided to discontinue the investigation into the Al-Yamamah contract, saying significant further inquiries lasting about 18 months would be needed and that the potential damage to the public interest, including national and international security, justified stopping it; he said the company and individuals involved denied any wrongdoing. The High Court ruled the discontinuance unlawful on April 10, 2008; the House of Lords reversed that ruling on July 30, 2008.
facts.quote: the Director of the Serious Fraud Office has decided to discontinue the investigation into the Al Yamamah contract

facts.claim: On March 1, 2010, BAE Systems plc pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to conspiring to defraud the United States, making false statements about its Foreign Corrupt Practices Act compliance program, and violating the Arms Export Control Act and ITAR, and was sentenced to a $400 million criminal fine. The DOJ's sentencing memorandum said that since 2005 the Department had examined suspicious payments by BAE in jurisdictions including the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Czech Republic and Hungary, certain of which formed the factual predicate for the conspiracy charge. BAE was not charged with bribery, and no individual was charged.
facts.quote: since 2005 the Department examined suspicious payments by BAES in numerous jurisdictions, including the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Czech Republic, and Hungary

facts.claim: A 2017 FBI memo, declassified under Executive Order 14040 and reported by CBS News, states that Omar al-Bayoumi received a monthly payment as a cooptee of Saudi General Intelligence, routed through then-Ambassador Prince Bandar bin Sultan. Saudi Arabia denies that al-Bayoumi was its asset.
facts.quote: al-Bayoumi received a monthly payment as a cooptee of Saudi General Intelligence, routed through then-Ambassador Prince Bandar bin Sultan

openQuestions: Bandar's appointment date (October 24, 1983) and the formal end of his term (September 2005) appear only in Wikipedia-derived results and are not recorded as facts; the owner may confirm them from the Saudi embassy or a wire report.

The 2007 Al-Yamamah allegations (BBC Panorama, the Guardian) are cited here through Newsweek, Time and Al Jazeera because the BBC and Guardian are unreachable by the search crawler. The PBS Frontline 2009 interview with Louis Freeh, speaking for Bandar, says the transfers to Riggs came from the UK Ministry of Defence rather than BAE; that account was not recorded as a fact.

No official U.S. or UK finding attributes bribery to Bandar: the SFO discontinued its inquiry, BAE's U.S. plea did not include a bribery charge, and no individual was charged. The site's pages should not state otherwise.

The site's 'Petrodollar Shield' node implies Riggs money reached 9/11 facilitators through Bandar. The documented record is the Haifa checks to Bassnan's wife (some passed to al-Bayoumi's wife) and the 1998 $15,000 check to Bassnan; the 9/11 Commission found no evidence these funds reached the conspiracy, and the 2017 FBI memo's 'routed through' statement concerns a GID payment to al-Bayoumi, not Riggs.
